sourceNote: Topic and subtopic headings, their numbering and the Core/Supplement split of every learning statement are transcribed from the official syllabus document. Learning-objective statements are our own paraphrase; each objective code is the subtopic code plus the board's own statement number (Core statements first, then Supplement). 'Supplement:' marks statements examined only on the Extended papers (2 and 4).
notes: Checked on 2026-10-08 against the official PDF (version 2, for exams in 2026, 2027 and 2028): the 6 topics, every numbered subtopic heading, the Core/Supplement split of every statement and the paper facts in the Assessment overview were read from the document's text.
Supplement-only subtopics (the Core column is empty): 1.6 Momentum and 4.5.2 The a.c. generator, linked to Papers 2 and 4. Core-only subtopics: 1.5.3, 1.7.2, 1.7.4, 2.1.1, 2.3.2, 4.2.5 and 4.4.

A node cannot restrict a concept by tier, so Supplement depth is recorded in the objectives ('Supplement:') and in the concept descriptions of content/concepts/physics-o.json; content written for Supplement statements must say so.
The syllabus gives the acceleration of free fall as approximately 9.8 m/s² (1.2.8); questions use g = 9.8 m/s² (9.8 N/kg) unless they state otherwise.

The 'Experimental skills (Papers 5 and 6)' node is ours, not a numbered subject-content topic: it holds the experimental-skills content (section 4 of the syllabus, AO3) so practical-skills questions can be tagged. Its objective codes (practical.n) are ours.

Not in this syllabus, though some other boards teach them: specific latent heat, thermometers, atmospheric pressure instruments, the equations of uniformly accelerated motion, machines, structures, engines and electronics beyond diodes and LEDs.
overview: Cambridge IGCSE Physics covers six topics: motion, forces and energy; thermal physics; waves (including light, the electromagnetic spectrum and sound); electricity and magnetism; nuclear physics; and space physics. Every topic has Core content for all candidates and Supplement content for Extended candidates, with an emphasis on applying physics to unfamiliar situations and on practical skills.
assessmentOverview: Core candidates take Paper 1 (45-minute multiple choice, 40 marks, 30%) and Paper 3 (75-minute theory, 80 marks, 50%); Extended candidates take Paper 2 (45-minute multiple choice, 40 marks, 30%) and Paper 4 (75-minute theory, 80 marks, 50%). Everyone also takes one practical paper: Paper 5 Practical Test (75 minutes) or Paper 6 Alternative to Practical (60 minutes), each 40 marks and 20%. Core candidates can achieve grades C to G; Extended candidates A* to G.

components.name: Paper 2: Multiple Choice (Extended)
components.description: 40 compulsory four-option multiple-choice items on the Core and Supplement content.

components.name: Paper 3: Theory (Core)
components.description: Short-answer and structured questions on the Core content.

components.name: Paper 4: Theory (Extended)
components.description: Short-answer and structured questions on the Core and Supplement content.

components.name: Paper 5: Practical Test
components.description: Practical tasks in a laboratory assessing the experimental skills of section 4. An alternative to Paper 6.

components.name: Paper 6: Alternative to Practical
components.description: Written questions on the experimental skills of section 4, with no experiments to carry out. An alternative to Paper 5.

routes.name: Core
routes.description: Papers 1 and 3 and one practical paper (5 or 6). Grades C to G are available.

routes.name: Extended
routes.description: Papers 2 and 4 and one practical paper (5 or 6). Grades A* to G are available.

objectives.text: Describe how rulers and measuring cylinders are used to measure a length or a volume.
Describe how clocks and digital timers are used to measure different time intervals.
Find an average value for a small distance or a short time by measuring many multiples, for example the period of a pendulum.
Supplement: explain the difference between a scalar (size only) and a vector (size and direction).
Supplement: identify distance, speed, time, mass, energy and temperature as scalars.
Supplement: identify force, weight, velocity, acceleration, momentum, electric field strength and gravitational field strength as vectors.
Supplement: find the resultant of two forces or two velocities at right angles, by calculation or by scale drawing.
Define speed as distance travelled per unit time and use v = s/t.
Define velocity as speed in a stated direction.
Calculate average speed as total distance travelled divided by total time taken.
Sketch, plot and interpret distance-time and speed-time graphs.
Decide from data or from the shape of a distance-time or speed-time graph whether an object is at rest, moving at constant speed, speeding up or slowing down.
Find speed from the gradient of a straight section of a distance-time graph.
Find the distance travelled from the area under a speed-time graph for constant speed or constant acceleration.
State that near the Earth's surface the acceleration of free fall g is roughly constant at about 9.8 m/s².
Supplement: define acceleration as change in velocity per unit time and use a = Δv/Δt.
Supplement: decide from data or a speed-time graph whether the acceleration is constant or changing.
Supplement: find acceleration from the gradient of a speed-time graph.
Supplement: treat a deceleration as a negative acceleration in calculations.
Supplement: describe how objects fall in a uniform gravitational field with and without air or liquid resistance, including terminal velocity.
State that mass measures the quantity of matter in an object at rest relative to the observer.
State that weight is the gravitational force on an object that has mass.
Define gravitational field strength as force per unit mass, use g = W/m and recognise that it equals the acceleration of free fall.
Know that a balance can be used to compare weights and masses.
Supplement: describe weight as the effect of a gravitational field on a mass and use this idea.
Define density as mass per unit volume and use ρ = m/V.
Describe how to find the density of a liquid, a regular solid and an irregular solid that sinks (volume by displacement), with the calculations.
Use density data to decide whether an object floats.
Supplement: use density data to decide whether one liquid floats on another liquid that it does not mix with.
Know that forces can change the size and shape of an object.
Sketch, plot and interpret load-extension graphs for an elastic solid and describe how the experiment is done.
Find the resultant of two or more forces acting along one straight line.
Know that an object stays at rest, or keeps moving in a straight line at constant speed, unless a resultant force acts on it.
State that a resultant force can change an object's velocity by changing its speed or its direction.
Describe friction between solid surfaces as a force that can oppose motion and cause heating.
Know that friction (drag) acts on an object moving through a liquid.
Know that friction (drag), such as air resistance, acts on an object moving through a gas.
Supplement: define the spring constant as force per unit extension and use k = F/x.
Supplement: define the limit of proportionality and identify it on a load-extension graph (the elastic limit is not required).
Supplement: use F = ma, knowing that the force and the acceleration are in the same direction.
Supplement: describe qualitatively circular motion caused by a force at right angles to the motion: how the force relates to speed, radius and mass.
Describe the moment of a force as its turning effect, with everyday examples.
Define and use moment = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot.
Apply the principle of moments with one force on each side of the pivot, including balancing a beam.
State that an object is in equilibrium when there is no resultant force and no resultant moment.
Supplement: apply the principle of moments when there is more than one force on each side of the pivot.
Supplement: describe an experiment showing that there is no resultant moment on an object in equilibrium.
Explain what the centre of gravity of an object is.
Describe an experiment to find the centre of gravity of an irregular plane lamina.
Describe qualitatively how the position of the centre of gravity affects the stability of simple objects.

children.name: Momentum
children.description: Supplement content only: examined on the Extended papers.

objectives.text: Supplement: define momentum as mass × velocity and use p = mv.
Supplement: define impulse as force × time for which it acts and use impulse = FΔt = Δ(mv).
Supplement: use conservation of momentum to solve simple problems in one dimension.
Supplement: define resultant force as the rate of change of momentum and use F = Δp/Δt.
Name the energy stores: kinetic, gravitational potential, chemical, elastic (strain), nuclear, electrostatic and internal (thermal).
Describe energy transfers between stores by forces (mechanical work), electric currents (electrical work), heating, and electromagnetic, sound and other waves.
Apply the principle of conservation of energy to simple examples, including simple flow diagrams.
Supplement: use Ek = ½mv² for kinetic energy.
Supplement: use ΔEp = mgΔh for the change in gravitational potential energy.
Supplement: apply conservation of energy to multi-stage examples, including Sankey diagrams.
Understand that mechanical or electrical work done equals the energy transferred.
Use W = Fd = ΔE for mechanical work.

Describe how useful energy or electricity is obtained from fossil fuels, biofuels, water (waves, tides, hydroelectric dams), geothermal sources, nuclear fuel and light from the Sun (solar cells and panels), and from wind.
Compare these methods in terms of renewability, availability, reliability, scale and environmental impact.
Understand qualitatively what the efficiency of an energy transfer means.
Supplement: know that radiation from the Sun is the main source of all our energy resources except geothermal, nuclear and tidal.
Supplement: know that the Sun releases energy by nuclear fusion.
Supplement: know that research aims to use nuclear fusion to generate electricity on a large scale.
Supplement: define and use percentage efficiency as useful energy (or power) output ÷ total energy (or power) input × 100%.
Define power as work done, or energy transferred, per unit time and use P = W/t and P = ΔE/t.
Define pressure as force per unit area and use p = F/A.
Describe how pressure depends on force and area in everyday situations.
Describe qualitatively how pressure under a liquid surface depends on depth and on the density of the liquid.
Supplement: use Δp = ρgΔh for the change in pressure beneath a liquid surface.
Know the properties that distinguish solids, liquids and gases.
Name the changes of state between solid, liquid and gas (gas to solid and solid to gas are not required).
Describe the arrangement, separation and motion of particles in solids, liquids and gases and draw simple particle diagrams.
Relate particle motion to temperature, including absolute zero (−273 °C) where particles have the least kinetic energy.
Explain gas pressure, and changes in it, by particles colliding with a surface.
Know that the random motion of microscopic particles in a suspension is evidence for the kinetic particle model.
Explain Brownian motion by random collisions between the microscopic particles and the particles of the liquid or gas.
Supplement: know that the forces and distances between particles, and their motion, determine the properties of solids, liquids and gases.
Supplement: explain gas pressure as the force per unit area produced by particles colliding with surfaces.
Supplement: know that light, fast-moving molecules can move microscopic particles, and distinguish atoms or molecules from microscopic particles.

children.name: Gases and the absolute scale of temperature

objectives.text: Explain with particles how the pressure of a fixed mass of gas changes when its temperature changes at constant volume, or its volume changes at constant temperature.
Convert between kelvin and degrees Celsius using T (K) = θ (°C) + 273.
Supplement: use pV = constant for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, including its graph.

children.name: Thermal expansion of solids, liquids and gases

objectives.text: Describe qualitatively the thermal expansion of solids, liquids and gases at constant pressure.
Describe everyday applications and consequences of thermal expansion.
Supplement: explain with particles why gases expand more than liquids, and liquids more than solids, for the same temperature rise.
Know that raising an object's temperature increases its internal energy.
Supplement: explain a temperature rise as an increase in the average kinetic energy of all the particles.
Supplement: define specific heat capacity as the energy needed per unit mass per unit temperature rise and use c = ΔE/(mΔθ).
Supplement: describe experiments to measure the specific heat capacity of a solid and of a liquid.
Describe melting and boiling as needing energy input with no change in temperature.
Know the melting and boiling points of water at standard atmospheric pressure.
Describe condensation and solidification in terms of particles.
Describe evaporation as the escape of the more energetic particles from a liquid's surface.
Know that evaporation cools a liquid.
Supplement: describe how boiling differs from evaporation.
Supplement: describe how temperature, surface area and air movement affect the rate of evaporation.
Supplement: explain how an object in contact with an evaporating liquid is cooled.
Describe experiments showing the properties of good thermal conductors and of thermal insulators.
Supplement: explain conduction in solids by lattice vibrations and, in metals, by free (delocalised) electrons.
Supplement: explain with particles why gases and most liquids are poor thermal conductors.
Supplement: know that many solids conduct better than insulators but worse than good conductors.
Know that convection is an important way thermal energy is transferred in liquids and gases.
Explain convection in liquids and gases by density changes and describe experiments that show it.
Know that thermal radiation is infrared radiation and that all objects emit it.
Know that thermal radiation does not need a medium.
Describe how surface colour (black or white) and texture (dull or shiny) affect the emission, absorption and reflection of infrared radiation.
Supplement: know that an object stays at constant temperature when it loses energy at the same rate as it gains it.
Supplement: know what happens to an object's temperature when it gains energy faster or slower than it loses it.
Supplement: know how the balance between incoming radiation and radiation emitted from the surface controls the Earth's temperature.
Supplement: describe experiments to compare good and bad emitters of infrared radiation.
Supplement: describe experiments to compare good and bad absorbers of infrared radiation.
Supplement: describe how the rate of emission depends on surface temperature and surface area.
Explain everyday applications and consequences of conduction, convection and radiation, such as heating a pan or heating a room by convection.
Supplement: explain more complex situations involving more than one method of transfer, such as a wood or coal fire and a car radiator.
Know that waves transfer energy without transferring matter.
Describe wave motion using vibrations in ropes and springs and experiments with water waves.
Describe wavefront, wavelength, frequency, crest, trough, amplitude and wave speed.
Use v = fλ.
Know that in a transverse wave the vibrations are at right angles to the direction of travel, as in electromagnetic, water and seismic S-waves.
Know that in a longitudinal wave the vibrations are parallel to the direction of travel, as in sound and seismic P-waves.
Describe reflection at a plane surface, refraction caused by a change of speed and diffraction through a narrow gap.
Describe how a ripple tank shows reflection, refraction (by a change of depth) and diffraction at a gap and at an edge.
Supplement: describe how wavelength and gap size affect diffraction through a gap.
Supplement: describe how wavelength affects diffraction at an edge.
Define and use the normal, the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection.
Describe how a plane mirror forms an image and its characteristics: same size, same distance behind the mirror, virtual.
State and use the law that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
Supplement: use simple constructions, measurements and calculations for plane mirrors.
Define and use the normal, the angle of incidence and the angle of refraction.
Describe an experiment showing refraction of light by transparent blocks of different shapes.
Describe how light passes through a transparent material at a boundary between two media.
State what is meant by the critical angle.
Describe internal reflection and total internal reflection with experimental and everyday examples.
Supplement: define refractive index as the ratio of the speeds of a wave in two different regions.
Supplement: use n = sin i / sin r.
Supplement: use n = 1 / sin c.
Supplement: describe the use of optical fibres, especially in telecommunications.
Describe how thin converging and diverging lenses act on a parallel beam of light.
Define and use focal length, principal axis and principal focus (focal point).
Draw and use ray diagrams for a real image formed by a converging lens.
Describe an image as enlarged, same size or diminished; upright or inverted; real or virtual.
Know that a virtual image is found by tracing diverging rays backwards and cannot be shown on a screen.
Supplement: draw and use ray diagrams for a virtual image formed by a converging lens.
Supplement: describe the use of a single lens as a magnifying glass.
Supplement: describe how converging and diverging lenses correct long sight and short sight.
Describe the dispersion of white light by a glass prism.
Know the seven traditional colours of the visible spectrum in order of frequency and of wavelength.
Supplement: know that light of a single frequency is called monochromatic.
Know the main regions of the electromagnetic spectrum in order of frequency and of wavelength.
Know that all electromagnetic waves travel at the same high speed in a vacuum.
Describe typical uses of each region, from radio and television transmission to medical uses of X-rays and gamma rays.
Describe the harmful effects of excessive exposure: microwaves heating body cells, infrared burns, ultraviolet damage to skin and eyes, and X-rays and gamma rays causing mutations and cancer.
Know that communication with artificial satellites is mainly by microwaves, using low-orbit and geostationary satellites.
Supplement: know that electromagnetic waves travel at 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum and at about the same speed in air.
Supplement: know how mobile phones, wireless internet, Bluetooth and optical fibres use electromagnetic radiation, and why each region suits its use.
Supplement: know the difference between digital and analogue signals.
Supplement: know that sound can be sent as a digital or an analogue signal.
Supplement: explain the benefits of digital signalling: faster data transmission and longer range thanks to accurate regeneration.
Describe how vibrating sources produce sound.
Describe sound waves as longitudinal.
State that humans hear frequencies from about 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz.
Know that sound needs a medium to travel through.
Know that the speed of sound in air is about 330-350 m/s.
Describe a method of finding the speed of sound in air by measuring a distance and a time.
Describe how amplitude and frequency affect the loudness and pitch of a sound.
Describe an echo as reflected sound.
Define ultrasound as sound above 20 kHz.
Supplement: describe compressions and rarefactions.
Supplement: know that sound generally travels fastest in solids and slowest in gases.
Supplement: describe uses of ultrasound in non-destructive testing, medical scanning of soft tissue and sonar, including depth and distance calculations.
Describe forces between magnetic poles and between magnets and magnetic materials, using the terms north and south pole, attraction, repulsion, magnetised and unmagnetised.
Describe induced magnetism.
State how temporary (soft iron) and permanent (steel) magnets differ.
Distinguish magnetic from non-magnetic materials.
Describe a magnetic field as a region where a magnetic pole feels a force.
Draw the field lines and their direction around a bar magnet.
State that the field direction at a point is the direction of the force on a north pole there.
Describe plotting field lines with a compass or iron filings and finding the field direction with a compass.
Describe uses of permanent magnets and electromagnets.
Supplement: explain magnetic forces as interactions between magnetic fields.
Supplement: know that closer field lines show a stronger field.
State that there are positive and negative charges.
State that like charges repel and unlike charges attract.
Describe simple experiments to produce charges by friction and to detect them.
Explain that charging by friction moves only negative charge (electrons).
Describe an experiment to tell electrical conductors from insulators.
Use a simple electron model to explain the difference between conductors and insulators, with examples.
Supplement: state that charge is measured in coulombs.
Supplement: describe an electric field as a region where a charge feels a force.
Supplement: state that the field direction is the direction of the force on a positive charge.
Supplement: describe the field patterns around a point charge, around a charged sphere and between two oppositely charged parallel plates.
Know that electric current is related to the flow of charge.
Describe using analogue and digital ammeters with different ranges.
Describe conduction in metals by the movement of free electrons.
Know the difference between direct current and alternating current.
Supplement: define current as charge passing a point per unit time and use I = Q/t.
Supplement: state that conventional current flows from positive to negative while electrons flow from negative to positive.
Define e.m.f. as the electrical work done by a source in moving unit charge around a complete circuit.
Know that e.m.f. is measured in volts.
Define potential difference as the work done by unit charge passing through a component.
Know that potential difference is measured in volts.
Describe using analogue and digital voltmeters with different ranges.
Supplement: use E = W/Q for e.m.f.
Supplement: use V = W/Q for potential difference.
Use R = V/I.
Describe how to find a resistance with a voltmeter and an ammeter and do the calculation.
State qualitatively how a metal wire's resistance depends on its length and cross-sectional area.
Supplement: sketch and explain current-voltage graphs for a fixed resistor, a filament lamp and a diode.
Supplement: use the facts that a metal conductor's resistance is proportional to its length and inversely proportional to its cross-sectional area.
Understand that circuits transfer energy from a source, such as a cell or the mains, to the components and then to the surroundings.
Use P = IV.
Use E = IVt.
Define the kilowatt-hour and calculate the cost of using appliances when energy is measured in kW h.

Draw and interpret circuit diagrams with cells, batteries, power supplies, generators, potential dividers, switches, fixed and variable resistors, heaters, NTC thermistors, light-dependent resistors, lamps, motors, ammeters, voltmeters, magnetising coils, transformers, fuses and relays.
Supplement: draw and interpret circuit diagrams with diodes and light-emitting diodes and know how they behave in a circuit.
Know that the current is the same everywhere in a series circuit.
Build and use series and parallel circuits.
Calculate the combined e.m.f. of several sources in series.
Calculate the combined resistance of resistors in series.
State that in a parallel circuit the current from the source is larger than the current in any branch.
State that two resistors in parallel have less resistance than either one alone.
State the advantages of wiring lamps in parallel in a lighting circuit.
Supplement: use in calculations that currents into a junction equal currents out, and that the p.d.s across series components add up to the total p.d.
Supplement: explain that the current into a junction equals the current out because charge is conserved.
Supplement: calculate the combined resistance of two resistors in parallel.

children.name: Action and use of circuit components

objectives.text: Know that, for a fixed current, the p.d. across a conductor increases as its resistance increases.
Supplement: describe how a variable potential divider works.
Supplement: use R1/R2 = V1/V2 for two resistors used as a potential divider.
State the hazards of damaged insulation, overheating cables, damp conditions and overloaded plugs, extension leads and sockets on the mains.
Know that a mains circuit has live, neutral and earth wires, and explain why the switch must be in the live wire.
Explain how trip switches and fuses work and choose suitable fuse ratings and trip settings.
Explain why an appliance's outer casing must be either double-insulated or earthed.
State that, for a double-insulated appliance without an earth wire, the fuse protects the circuit and cables.
Know that an e.m.f. is induced in a conductor that moves across a magnetic field or is linked by a changing field.
Describe an experiment demonstrating electromagnetic induction.
State the factors that affect the size of an induced e.m.f.
Supplement: know that the induced e.m.f. opposes the change that causes it.
Supplement: state and use the relative directions of force, field and induced current.

children.name: The a.c. generator
children.description: Supplement content only: examined on the Extended papers.

objectives.text: Supplement: describe a simple a.c. generator (rotating coil or rotating magnet), with slip rings and brushes where needed.
Supplement: sketch and interpret graphs of e.m.f. against time for a simple a.c. generator and link the coil's position to the peaks, troughs and zeros.
Describe the pattern and direction of the field around a straight wire and a solenoid carrying a current.
Describe an experiment to find these field patterns and their direction.
Describe how relays and loudspeakers use the magnetic effect of a current, with examples.
Supplement: state qualitatively how the field strength varies around a straight wire and a solenoid.
Supplement: describe how changing the size and direction of the current changes the field.
Describe an experiment showing the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field, including reversing the current and the field.
Supplement: recall and use the relative directions of force, field and current.
Supplement: find the direction of the force on a beam of charged particles in a magnetic field.
Know that a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field can feel a turning effect, increased by more turns, more current or a stronger field.
Supplement: describe how an electric motor works, including the split-ring commutator and brushes.
Describe the construction of a simple transformer with a soft-iron core.
Use the terms primary, secondary, step-up and step-down.
Use Vp/Vs = Np/Ns.
Describe the use of transformers for high-voltage transmission of electricity.
State the advantages of high-voltage transmission.
Supplement: explain how a simple iron-cored transformer works.
Supplement: use IpVp = IsVs for a 100% efficient transformer.
Supplement: use P = I²R to explain why cable losses are smaller at higher voltage.

children.name: The nuclear model of the atom

objectives.text: Describe an atom as a positively charged nucleus with negatively charged electrons orbiting it.
Know how atoms become positive ions by losing electrons or negative ions by gaining them.
Supplement: describe how alpha-particle scattering by thin metal foil supports the nuclear model: a tiny nucleus in mostly empty space, holding most of the mass and positive charge.
Describe the nucleus as made of protons and neutrons.
State the relative charges of the proton, neutron and electron as +1, 0 and -1.
Define proton number Z and nucleon number A and calculate the number of neutrons.
Use nuclide notation.
Explain what an isotope is and that an element can have several isotopes.
Supplement: describe fission and fusion as the splitting and joining of nuclei, with nuclide equations and a qualitative account of mass and energy changes.
Supplement: relate the proton number to the relative charge on a nucleus.
Supplement: relate the nucleon number to the relative mass of a nucleus.
Know what background radiation is.
Know the main sources of background radiation: radon gas, rocks and buildings, food and drink, and cosmic rays.
Know that ionising radiation is measured with a detector connected to a counter.
Use count rates in counts per second or counts per minute.
Supplement: use measurements of background radiation to find a corrected count rate.

children.name: The three types of nuclear emission

objectives.text: Describe nuclear emission as spontaneous and random in direction.
Identify alpha, beta and gamma emissions by their nature, relative ionising effect and relative penetrating ability.
Supplement: describe how alpha particles, beta particles and gamma rays are deflected in electric and magnetic fields.
Supplement: explain their relative ionising effects using kinetic energy and charge.
Know that radioactive decay is a random, spontaneous change in an unstable nucleus that can emit alpha or beta particles and/or gamma rays.
State that alpha or beta decay changes the nucleus into that of a different element.
Supplement: know that an isotope can be radioactive because of too many neutrons or because the nucleus is too heavy.
Supplement: describe how alpha decay, beta decay and gamma emission change the nucleus, including beta decay turning a neutron into a proton and an electron.
Supplement: write decay equations in nuclide notation for alpha, beta and gamma emission.
Define half-life and use it in simple calculations, including data in tables and decay curves.
Supplement: find half-life from data or decay curves where background radiation has not been subtracted.
Supplement: explain how the type of radiation and the half-life decide which isotope suits smoke alarms, food irradiation, sterilisation, thickness measurement and tracers.
State the effects of ionising radiation on living things: cell death, mutations and cancer.
Describe how radioactive materials are moved, used and stored safely.
Supplement: explain safety precautions in terms of reducing exposure time, increasing distance and using shielding.
Use the Earth's tilted rotation once in about 24 hours to explain the Sun's apparent daily motion and day and night.
Use the Earth's orbit of the Sun in about 365 days to explain the seasons.
Use the Moon's orbit of the Earth in about a month to explain its cycle of phases.
Supplement: define and use average orbital speed v = 2πr/T.
Describe the Solar System: the Sun, the eight planets in order, minor planets such as dwarf planets and asteroids, moons and comets.
Know that the four inner planets are small and rocky and the four outer planets large and gaseous, and explain this with the accretion model.
Know that the gravitational field at a planet's surface depends on its mass and that the field weakens with distance.
Calculate how long light takes to travel large distances, such as between objects in the Solar System.
Know that the Sun holds most of the Solar System's mass, which is why the planets orbit it.
Know that the Sun's gravitational attraction keeps objects in orbit around it.
Supplement: know that planets, minor planets and comets have elliptical orbits with the Sun not at the centre unless the orbit is nearly circular.
Supplement: analyse planetary data on orbital distance, orbital period, density, surface temperature and surface gravitational field strength.
Supplement: know that the Sun's field and the planets' orbital speeds decrease with distance from the Sun.
Supplement: know that a body in an elliptical orbit moves faster near the Sun and explain this using conservation of energy.
Know that the Sun is a medium-sized star of mostly hydrogen and helium that radiates mainly infrared, visible light and ultraviolet.
Supplement: know that stable stars are powered by the fusion of hydrogen into helium.
State that galaxies contain many billions of stars, that the Sun is in the Milky Way, that other stars are much further away than the Sun, and that light-years measure these distances.
Supplement: know that one light-year is 9.5 × 10¹⁵ m.
Supplement: describe the life cycle of a star from an interstellar cloud and protostar through a stable star to a red giant or supergiant and a white dwarf, supernova, neutron star or black hole.
Know that the Milky Way is one of billions of galaxies and is about 100 000 light-years across.
Describe redshift as an increase in the observed wavelength of radiation from receding stars and galaxies.
Know that light from distant galaxies is redshifted compared with light emitted on the Earth.
Know that redshift from distant galaxies shows the Universe is expanding and supports the Big Bang theory.
Supplement: know that cosmic microwave background radiation (CMBR) of a particular frequency is observed in every direction.
Supplement: explain that the CMBR was produced shortly after the Universe formed and has been stretched into the microwave region by expansion.
Supplement: know that a galaxy's speed away from the Earth can be found from the redshift of its starlight.
Supplement: know that the distance to a far galaxy can be found from the brightness of a supernova in it.
Supplement: define the Hubble constant H0 = v/d and use the equation.
Supplement: know that the current estimate of H0 is 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ per second.
Supplement: know that d/v = 1/H0 estimates the age of the Universe and supports the idea that all matter began at a single point.

topics.name: Experimental skills (Papers 5 and 6)
topics.description: Not a numbered subject-content topic: section 4 of the syllabus (Practical assessment, AO3) lists the experimental skills assessed in Paper 5 (Practical Test) and Paper 6 (Alternative to Practical).

objectives.text: Plan an experiment or investigation, identifying the variables to change, measure and control.
Choose and use apparatus correctly and safely, taking readings to an appropriate precision.
Record observations and measurements in tables with headings and units.
Plot graphs, draw best-fit lines and work out gradients and intercepts.
Interpret data, draw conclusions and identify anomalous results.
Evaluate methods and suggest improvements and precautions.
